Be that as it may, I think we may now realize the Grammatical opportunities and embarrassments we encounter as we arrive in our Kantian system at a transcendent realm composed of things-in-themselves. Whatever it may be cosmologically, a thing in itself is Grammatically a thing without reference to context. And for our purposes, that is as far as we need go. Grammatically, then, the transcendent realm is a realm of things-without-context, or things-without-relation.

What does that give us? First, note that relations are "determinations." They assign borders (termini) to a thing. A synonym is "conditions," since "conditions" are likewise contextual, as with the conditions of an organism's existence. Without worrying greatly what it may mean in the literal sense, but merely considering the Grammatical resources available here, let us note that, as the empirical realm is the realm of the determined or conditioned^ and the transcendental realm is the realm of the conditions that provided the terms (determinations), so the transcendent realm of things-in-themselves would be the realm of the undetermined or unconditioned. Whereupon, lo! we find ourselves in a realm of freedomI And so, we have come upon a scene that allows for the possibility of action.

The transcendental had transcended the empirical; it had raised us to a level of generalization that "necessarily" unified the world of particulars, infusing the world of particulars with its spirit. And so now in turn the transcendent has transcended the transcendental, thereby infusing the world of determinism with the spirit of freedom (which is another way of saying that we have added to the world of physical motion the possibilities of moral action).

However, since we began our enterprise with all respect for the requirements of empirical science, we have defined knowledge by pirical tests. Knowledge by definition, then, is the knowledge of ditions and relations. It is the knowledge of appearances, the knowledge of objects as they necessarily appear when seen in terms of our human categories (the categories of the mind in general). So, by defiemcon-

nition, the transcendent realm of the unconditoned things-in-themselves (the scene that contains the possibilities of freedom) cannot be known. Hence, we must restrict the claims we can make about it. But whereas it can't be known, it can be thought about, for we are now thinking about it.

Modern positivists would question whether this statement has meaning; it is certainly "non-sense" if we interpret that word literally, for it is a statement about a realm outside the realm of sensory experience. But if you consider it purely from the standpoint of Grammatical resources, it is obvious that a word as highly generalized as "the conditioned" leaves us with "the unconditioned" as its dialectical opposite, hence as the only term left to be the ground or context of the conditioned. And though we certainly cannot \now this ground, in the scientific meaning which we have given to "knowledge," we can "think" it in recognizing that, so far as the patterns of human thought are concerned, the only term that could antithetically match the "conditioned" would be the "unconditioned." And the unknown to which we thus refer in so basic a pattern of human thought might be characterized as "thought of."

It is an important spot to haggle over, however, if you are going to haggle at all. For once you let this point go by unquestioned, you give Kant some important advantages. Paper need not know the meaning of fire in order to burn. But in the "idea" offire there is a persuasive ingredient. By this route something of the rhetorical motive comes to lurk in every "meaning" however purely "scientific" its pretensions. Wherever there is persuasion, there is rhetoric. And wherever there is "meaning," there is "persuasion." Food, eaten and digested, is not rhetorical. But in the meaning o[food there is much rhetoric, the meaning being persuasive enough for the idea of food to be used, like the ideas ofreligion, as a rhetorical device of statesmen. (RM 172-73)

This passage seems far from clear. Additionally, the numerous ironizing quotation marks and italics indicate various forms of pressure and stress. The word meaning, not insignificantly, is italicized twice and twice placed in quotation marks. What does meaning mean here? The most direct reading would be that Burke understands meaning to emerge as our ideas about the world, making meaning the sense or significance of things, events, and relations. Meaning is gleaned from the symbolicity that drapes over (or maybe permeates) the mundane world, circulating it as the significance available to us. The mention of science is important here, for Burke is clearly dissatisfied with a positivist, scientific claim of mere facticity for things of the world, as if measuring qualia sufficed for generating meaning. Thus, he will grant that paper, being paper, has no ideas as such; its rapid oxidation at temperatures around 451 degrees Fahrenheit is a purely chemical reaction. But to remain at this level is to willfully (or methodologically) remain at observation degree zero, and it obscures fire's role in human affairs. When Bradbury's Fireman comes to

burn the books, though, we move into a different realm, one of meaning, and we see that fire is a full rhetorical participant. Fire, then, is more than just a sensed material phenomenon; its integration into the human world necessitates ideas. These ideas mean, and insofar as they mean, they bodily invoke, and insofar as they bodily invoke, they persuade.

As I observed in my discussion of Hawhee, this is not an abstract notion of fire as meaningful; rather, it is one entirely grounded in the bodily integration of ideas stemming from physical experience. As Burke puts it in Attitudes toward History, "our primeval ancestors, by learning language, no longer experienced a sensation solely as a sensation" (382). As he goes on to explain, we may like the warmth ofa fire, and such warmth is certainly a sensation, but as soon as we start putting such experience into language, the words come to "tell a story"; as a result, attitudes (or affective stances) can emerge and be deployed across various forms of discursive interaction, such as the movement from "that feels warm" to the observation that someone is "warm-hearted" (Burke,AH383).

This elevation of meaning over mundane, objective matter is further evinced in other passages. Later in A Rhetoric of Motives Burke again discusses the effect of material phenomena. This time he calls them a form of intuition, and he then tethers intuition to a notion of infancy. Dwelling, then, entails more than existing and subsisting; it extends beyond simply doing what we need to do-working, socializing, building-to survive to include the richness that is developed and pursued in how we are doing so. Building is not just construction, notjust technics. Nor is it isolable, except at cost, from ambient concerns. To understand place in terms of building necessitates the fullest possible understanding of what makes a location a location. As Heidegger goes on to explain, the fourfold is already wrought with the building of the farmhouse, since the building ofit, which sprang from dwelling, is already a located response to and a living with the fourfold. The farmhouse is built from and sustained by what the earth gives

and lies nestled in the earth's hollows; it receives its direction and temporality from the sky and is further sustained by what the sky brings; the divinities are traced in thankfulness and respect, fear and hope; and death and birth and all the cares of mortals are knit into the house and responsive to the other three aspects of the fourfold, as each of the others similarly join together. None of these things is present in any simple and direct manner. but they can all be seen as gathered in the way of life that gave rise to the farmhouse. Thus, the fourfold cannot be reduced to direct presence, as it is also what remains concealed, although we too often take the mundane persistence of presence as all there is, since it is most near to our everyday concerns. Place is never given in its entirety.

But here we come to the crucial point. This withdrawing is also a form of supporting; it is the repletion of all that is, which in turn ensures that the world is always more than what we make ofit. If the world is to make claims ,on us, ifwe are to dwell in such manner as to attune ourselves to what is noninstrumental. nonrepresentational, then this withdrawal becomes es- :sential. In other words, human knowledge is al ways only partial, and rather tha1\ see this as an invitation to extend knowledge further, as ifwe could pry open all mystery and have it stand revealed before us, Heidegger argues that what remains unconcealed is itself valuable. Dwelling makes being's concealment an occasion for joy and humbleness, thought and insight, guidance and action. It grants the world a kind of meaning or value that, while it cannot speak directly (and hence is neither meaning nor value, exactly), nevertheless calls us in its holding sway and conditions every aspect of our being together. This is the productive "acknowledgment of what is not human in the context of what is" (Thiele, Timely 179). Thus, a location is inseparable from its unique expanse and its ecological connectedness to larger surroundings; all take part in making place a place. Human building arises from place, of course, and is a further disclosure of place, but Heidegger seems to indicate that there is something sound and hale in attuning ourselves to place's role in our constructive pursuits rather than seeking only human-derived, technical, or efficiency-driven projects. I will explore this idea further in the next chapter.

As part of his engagement with technology, the later Heidegger developed a rich notion of dwelling. Dwelling as he uses it entails an ecological attunement to the environment, although it will mean more than this. It differs from, say, the idea that we all have worldviews, which would make dwelling a matter of properly tempering our cultural knowledge. Worldviews, as I have argued, posit a more or less stable common reality variously shaping or shaped by human culture and language. The notion of worldviews invokes the subjective, writ large as society, and thereby gives over to (Western) science the authority to pronounce the truth of nature. A worldview thus constitutes how the world appears "out theren as colored by cultural lenses, a position that insinuates a disengagement between people and world, so that ultimately "objective" reason becomes the means to eliminate cultural distortion and get at the actual essence of things (Ingold 15). 2 As Heidegger argues, however, dwelling indicates not a worldview but a principle of being: culture is materially enworlded. That is, dwelling is a way of being conditioned and permeated by things so that they are inseparable from what it means to live in the world. But dwelling also has a hermeneutic character, in that, like Dasein, questions

of being are continually at issue (see Heidegger, BT 32). The question of how existence is best pursued is not simply given as knowledge but achieved through continual questioning. Such questioning and formulating does not reside solely with the human. Thus, dwelling is not mere survival or existence, nor is it the layering of culture over mundane reality. Dwelling is characterized by thriving or "flourishing" conceived in an ecological key (Heidegger, DT 47). It is not simply an ensemble of practices or habits whose daily performance gets marked by the style we then associate with a particular community. Rather, dwelling indicates lived relations woven into complex ecologies of the world's things and forces. This is not passive coexistence or simple adaptation to things; it is an active if conditioned comportment toward the world. Indeed, this is why Heidegger connects dwelling with building (PLT 146, 148).3By doing so, he grounds human flourishing in constructive activity. That is, the attunement to the world that characterizes dwelling is not passivity. Rather, it is activity that works through and with things as they show up in the world alongside us. Heidegger characterizes this relationship as a dynamic kind of''letting ben appearing as forms of shepherding, cultivating, sparing, and ca retaking (PLT 147-48).

Heidegger's terminology is overly rustic, an important and not unproblematic consideration. Heidegger incorporated such attitudes into much of his thought. When he turned to technological artifacts in his critical ruminations on technology, he often found them to lack a special status he reserved for "things," which were as often as not illustrated through rustic examples. A wine jug is a thing, but a river dam is an object, and in the later Heidegger, the "object" label conveys a negative valuation. I think we must resist this valuation but not simply reject it. Rather, we might ask what stakes lie in making a distinction between a thing and an object. Can this distinction tells us anything that bears on rhetoric and its relation to things and how we dwell with them, even as we move past the limitations we recognize in Heidegger's particular articulation of this distinction? These questions indicate that Heidegger's romanticizations are more than evocations of the rustic. In order to explain this, I want to look at what Heidegger has to say about things and, in particular, how he wants to grant to the thing, as opposed to the object, the ability to manifest what he calls the fourfold (das Geviert). The fourfold is the gathering of earth, sky, mortals, and gods-admittedly a rather oblique statement. results.text:
My arguments for the importance of ambience should not be understood as any simple call to "pay attention." One is in any event only partially aware of ongoing events within one's environs at any given time. The environs are ready-to-hand, yes, but they now have agentive powers Heidegger's hammer never had. Emile A arts and Stefano Marzano point out, "As technology becomes hidden within these static, unintelligent objects, they will become subjects, active and intelligent actors in our environment ... [and the] immaterial world of our interactions with them-services, games, entertainment, information, communication-will become more prominent in our lives" (8-9). Greenfield argues that ubiquitous computing "will disturb unwritten agreements about workspace and homespace, the presentation of self and the right to privacy. It contains an inherent, unsettling potential for panoptical surveillance, regulation, and 'rationalization.' Its presence in our lives will transfigure our notions of space and time, self and other, citizen and society in ways we haven't begun to contemplate" (3). In short, ambient intelligence radically changes who we are in our environs; it

situates us differently in the world, evoking other ways of being. It thereby also reveals rhetoric to us differently than it has appeared heretofore. Ambience thus teaches us that we cannot rely solely on salience, attention, and consciousness to guide us.

Rhetoric has much to learn from music on this score. I am claiming that ambient music is an important development, both in its own right as a form of thinking (and not simply as expression ofhuman thought and affect) and as something that shows how the power of place and the agency of technology become integral not just to the music's creation but to what we take the music to be. Music is not just the salience of its affective work. Ambient music has still other rhetorical dimensions, including politics. It has ramifications for how we dwell in the world. Eno claims that ambient music is directly political: "The decision to stop seeing yourself as the centre of the world, to see yourself as part of the greater flow of things, as having limited options and responsibility for your actions[.] ... that is political theory: and it's where the music grows from" (qtd. in Tamm 91).

It is hardly a stretch to see that these political insights resonate with the extension of digital computing into things and environs. As Eno is quite aware, there are both opportunities and dangers here, which is why transforming how one sees oneself in the world is integral to a politics attuned to these dangers. 21 So, much as ambient music does, ubiquitous computing (ambient intelligence) showcases how the power of place and the agency of technology become integral not just to our everyday activity but to a conception of dynamic life itself. We need not overstate the case by claiming we are on the threshold of a brave new world. Rather, we are simply seeing capacities, implications, and energies as previously assembled now giving way to vibrant and different intensities and assemblages. But we cannot ignore how these different forms also assemble new forms oflife, or new ways of being-in-the-world.

Rhetoric, Ambience, Dwelling

We need conceptions ofrhetoric that keep pace with these transformations and their attendant opportunities and dangers, that not only help us make sense of them but enable us to flourish (and that will, of course, spur new transformations). We do not need a new rhetoric, however; rather, we must work anew with what has been brought forward in rhetorical theory and practice. Rhetoric is revealing and doing-doing as revealing and revealing as doing-and hence integral to our dwelling in the world. It can no longer be understood solely as a subjective, verbal, visual, or even performative

Theoretically concocted 'explanations' of the Being-present-at-hand of Others urge themselves upon us all too easily ; but over against such explanations we must hold fast to the pheno­ menal facts of the case which we have pointed out, namely, that Others are encountered environmentally. This elemental worldly kind of encountering, which belongs to Dasein and is closest to it, goes so far that even one's own Dasein becomes something that it can itself proximally 'come across' only when it looks away from 'Experiences' and the 'centre of its actions', or does not as yet 'see' them at all. Dasein finds 'itself' proximally in what it does, uses, expects, avoids-in those things environmentally ready­ to-hand with which it is proximally concerned. And even when Dasein explicitly addresses itself as "I here", this locative personal designation must be understood in terms of Dasein's existential spatiality. In Interpreting this (See Section 23) we have already intimated that this "1-here" does not mean a certain privileged point-that of an !-Thing-but is to be understood as Being-in in terms of the "yonder" of the world that is ready-to-hand-the "yonder" which is the dwelling-place of Dasein as concern.1 W. von Humboldtll has alluded to certain languages which express the 
'I' by 'here', the 'thou' by 'there', the 'he' by 'yonder', thus rendering the personal pronouns by locative adverbs, to put it grammatically. It is con­ troversial whether indeed the primordial signification of locative expres­ sions is adverbial or pronominal. But this dispute loses its basis if one notes that locative adverbs have a relationship to the "I" qua Dasein. The
